source.title: Minimax-optimal Scaling Laws in Ridge Regression via Transfer Learning
source.authors: Yalda Shabanzadeh; Diyuan Wu; Marco Mondelli

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends transfer-scaling analysis to language-model fine-tuning and reports target test-loss results for GPT-2 small.
record.gate_note: The directly relevant results are the language-model experiments in Section 6 and Appendix E.2. The synthetic regression theory and cited results are not evidence about language-model pretraining scaling. The paper reports language-model loss curves in Figure 3, but gives no numerical curve values in the text.
record.test_reason: The study derives power-law transfer-risk rates in regression and tests their predictions synthetically, bearing on V5. Its regression results and language-model comparisons also show that scaling rates depend on regularization, source-data growth and target optimization, bearing on V7. Faster fine-tuning than training from scratch alone does not establish downstream predictability under V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the language-model conclusion but omits the main regression conclusions. The authors derive deterministic-equivalent transfer-risk scaling laws, show that their optimized exponent matches the joint minimax rate in the transfer-gain regime, and prove the same expected-risk exponent for suitably scheduled one-pass SGD. A target-independent source regularization attains these rates. Language-model results suggest related transfer phenomena whose rate advantage depends on source growth and target optimization.
record.recipe_differences: The LM experiment uses GPT-2 small trained on FineWeb-Edu and fine-tuned on Python; it compares target-only, source-only, fine-tuning, and an L2-SP implementation rather than reproducing either original scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported transfer advantage changes with source-budget growth and with target-training length/optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning has lower target loss at small budgets and target-only training subsequently closes the gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining can improve target-data efficiency, with an advantage that diminishes as target data increases.

record.problems: The language-model experiment uses one model size, one source distribution and one target distribution, and only three seeds. Figure 3 does not provide numerical curve values in the text; the reported scaling conclusions concern local rates over the tested target-budget range.
record.rows_left_out: No reported outcome-bearing language-model curves in Figure 3 were left out. Individual plotted values are retained as figure-only rows because the text does not state their numbers.

untested.parts: No controlled test of bottleneck-free language-model pretraining loss over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fits predicting runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute optimization of model size and token allocation.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.

The language-model experiment does not establish a global power-law fit; its six unique-token budgets span a factor of 32. Image-feature experiments test deterministic-equivalent accuracy for synthetic regression labels, not image-model loss scaling.
No validated prediction of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss. The reported transfer advantages and local loss slopes do not establish that predictive relationship.
No comparison of published language-model laws, parameter-counting conventions, fitting estimators or compute-optimal parameter/token splits.

missing.what: Theorem 3's transfer-risk scaling exponent and its dependence on source/target spectra, signal and regularization. These are the study's own results, unlike the recalled minimax theorem.

Corollary 1's minimax exponent (δ−1+γn)/δ and target-independent source regularization. Explicitly distinguish the proved deterministic-equivalent rate from the conjectured matching actual ridge-risk rate.
missing.locator: Section 5.3, Corollary 1 and discussion following equation (29)

missing.what: The proved expected-risk power law for one-pass SGD with the specified source regularization and geometric learning-rate schedule.

Synthetic empirical confirmation of predicted risk rates, including bias-limited, variance-limited and optimally tuned transfer conditions; a=2, b=6, rtr=0.6, d=50,000, target samples 2^7–2^12, 50 seeds.

record.verdict_notes: No numerical curve values were inferred from the text extraction. Missing global fits are untested evidence, not a demonstrated failure of power-law form. No V5 verdict rests solely on a transfer method outperforming its baselines.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over language-model parameter count, pretraining tokens, or compute measuring held-out pretraining loss.
No small-run power-law fits or tests predicting much larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep optimizing parameter and token allocation.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.

Tests transfer/fine-tuning for one GPT-2 small model and one source-target setup; does not test other modalities, repeated data, or a range of model sizes. Does not establish a single power-law fit across several orders of magnitude.
Measures target-domain test loss against target-token budgets in one model and setup; does not test a broad set of downstream tasks, model sizes, or predictability from pretraining loss.
No analysis of the original laws’ fitted exponents or compute-optimal split as a function of fitting choices.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared target test loss over target-token budgets for transfer and non-transfer training procedures.
rows.baseline: Target-only training; source-only training is also compared in the study.
rows.value: The text reports that fine-tuning has lower loss at small target budgets, while target-only training gradually closes the gap.
rows.note: Qualitative result; no individual loss values are stated.
rows.check: The reported transfer advantage and closing gap do not determine whether loss follows a power law. Target budgets are unique tokens from 2^21 to 2^26.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared target test-loss scaling as source budget grows with target budget under short target training.
rows.measure: Target test-loss rate over target-token budgets
rows.value: Fine-tuning can decrease faster over the early scaling range; the text reports a higher fine-tuning rate than target-only and source-only training overall.
rows.note: The text describes an early-range rate advantage, not a fitted power law over several orders of magnitude.
rows.check: The early local-rate advantage is conditional on source-budget growth and short target training; it does not establish one power-law form. It directly bears on setup dependence under V7.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared target test-loss scaling after additional target optimization.

conditions.value: multiple epochs, selected using validation loss

rows.measure: Target test-loss rate over target-token budgets
rows.value: The fine-tuning rate advantage becomes smaller after additional target optimization.
rows.note: This is an explicit qualification of the transfer advantage.
rows.check: Observed applies to V7: additional target optimization weakens the rate advantage. The power-law form under V5 remains undetermined.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared fine-tuning and fine-tuning with L2-SP against target-only and source-only training.

conditions.value: one pass and validation-selected multiple epochs

rows.measure: Target test loss and local loss exponent
rows.value: The authors report a higher fine-tuning rate overall, but say its advantage depends on target optimization.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors across seeds are reported for ratios and differences; individual values not stated.
rows.note: The paper defines local exponents between neighboring target budgets and also fits exponents over longer windows.
rows.check: This aggregates methods and conditions already covered by Q1–Q3 and the figure rows. Split actual exponent estimates by method, source growth and optimization. Appendix E.2 describes uncertainty calculations but supplies no numerical estimates or standard errors.

relationships.condition: Transfer regression with shared coefficients, commuting power-law covariance spectra and the stated signal assumptions
relationships.reason: Text-based, missing rows: Theorem 3 derives polynomial risk-equivalent rates up to logarithmic factors; Figure 1 reports empirical recovery of those rates.
relationships.display_finding: Derived polynomial risk-equivalent rates held up to logarithmic factors and were recovered empirically.

relationships.condition: Ridge pretraining followed by suitably scheduled one-pass SGD, δ > 1 and γc < γn < 1
relationships.reason: Text-based, missing row: Lemma 1 establishes expected target excess risk of order n^(-(δ−1+γn)/δ), up to logarithmic factors.
relationships.display_finding: Expected target excess risk scaled as n^(-(δ−1+γn)/δ), up to logarithmic factors.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 small, FineWeb-Edu to Python, growing source budgets and different target-training lengths
relationships.reason: Q2 and Q3 report an early rate advantage under short training that weakens with additional target optimization.
relationships.display_finding: GPT-2 small showed an early scaling-rate advantage during short Python training after FineWeb-Edu transfer, which weakened with additional target optimization.

relationships.condition: Power-law transfer regression with different source and target regularization schedules
relationships.reason: Text-based, missing rows: Theorem 3 and Figure 1 show scaling exponents changing with regularization through bias and variance bottlenecks.
relationships.display_finding: Source and target regularization schedules changed scaling exponents through bias and variance bottlenecks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2 small transfer/fine-tuning, especially short target training
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports faster early target-loss decrease under growing source budgets, consistent with transfer scaling in this tested setting (Q2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2 small with additional target optimization
reader_labels.reason: The rate advantage weakens after extra optimization, and the experiment does not establish one power law across several orders of magnitude (Q3, Q4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fixed source budget and small target budgets; also short target training with growing source budget
reader_labels.reason: Fine-tuning is reported to have lower loss at small target budgets and a faster early loss decrease in the growing-source setting (Q1, Q2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Target-only training gradually closes the fixed-source gap, and the reported transfer rate advantage is weaker after additional target optimization (Q1, Q3).
